transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-18
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jonah Kim (Alder Arc CTO), Priya Desai (Alder Arc Infra), Miguel Santos (Alder Arc Partnerships), Sofie Laurent (Security)

[00:00] Ethan Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we can dive in. I'm Ethan, account lead on the Redwood side, joining with Priya Rao, our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Jonah Kim: Good, thanks. Excited to chat — we're trying to get a sense of how Redwood would map onto our cloud GPU pools.
[00:17] Priya Rao: Awesome. Quick agenda from our side: network patterns and VPC peering, AMI/image compatibility, quantization profiles and perf, and then an outline of a short pilot. Feel free to jump in.
[00:27] Miguel Santos: Sounds good. Also curious about business flow — like how Dedicated vs hosted would look when using Alder Arc as an onramp.
[00:33] Ethan Morales: Totally. We'll cover that — high level: Redwood Dedicated can route by policy to partner GPU pools; list of options is direct VPC peering, shared transit, or a reverse VPN tunnel depending on customer's network posture.
[00:45] Sofie Laurent: Quick security callout: we need to make sure there's KMS parity, key wrapping, and audit logs. We'll ask more later.
[00:52] Priya Desai: For our infra team, a lot depends on whether Redwood needs root on the instance or if a container runtime will suffice. We usually provide an AMI with our drivers.

[01:10] Priya Rao: Yeah — Redwood prefers running our runtime as a container on top of your AMI, but we do have an optional AMI image for tight-integrations. The biggest items for us are kernel driver compatibility and whether your nodes expose the NVLink topology for multi-GPU models.
[01:28] Jonah Kim: NVLink is exposed, but it's behind our proprietary fabric — sometimes drivers need specific flags. We can share the AMI spec.

[02:05] [00:120] Ethan Morales: Can you also share the typical image/driver versions? We do some auto-selection of kernels at startup, and mismatches can cause perf regressions.
[02:15] Jonah Kim: Sure. Currently we're on 530.x driver family, and our CUDA builds are 12.2 on most pools. We also have an older pool with 11.8 for legacy customers.
[02:25] Priya Rao: Good to know. That maps to our compatibility matrix — we've validated with CUDA 12.x in lab but it's always good to test on your exact AMI.

[03:00] Miguel Santos: On the business flow — if a Redwood customer picks Alder Arc as a capacity option, who handles billing?
[03:08] Ethan Morales: Typical pattern is partner-billed or split via marketplace — but for the pilot we can do a partner-billed sandbox. That avoids procurement friction. We'll loop in GTM later.

[03:40] [00:200] Priya Desai: Network-wise, we prefer AWS-style VPC peering or transit gateway for low-latency. Our cluster is in a dedicated VPC. Can Redwood initiate a peering or do you prefer us to?
[03:50] Priya Rao: Either works. We usually request the partner create the peering from their side so we can attach to our control plane; we provide a short runbook. For stricter customers we can also do a reverse tunnel.

[04:20] Jonah Kim: One of our customers asked about on-prem-like private deployments — i.e., air-gapped scenarios. Is Redwood Private relevant here?
[04:28] Ethan Morales: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem and VPC with a customer-managed control plane. But that tends to be an enterprise engagement with licensing. For now pilot = staging cluster connectivity.

[04:50] [00:300] Sofie Laurent: Security: we need to confirm encryption at rest and transit plus key management. Alder Arc uses a custody KMS; will Redwood accept a partner-managed KMS?
[04:58] Priya Rao: We support external KMS via key-wrap — we can integrate with your KMS/HSM. For the pilot we can run in a sandbox with keys we control. For an enterprise production roll we'll do a KMS integration and SOC mapping.

[05:25] Jonah Kim: Great. On to model compatibility — our ops team will want to know if Redwood's runtime supports int8 or 4-bit quantization without modifying model artifacts.
[05:34] Priya Rao: Redwood runtime supports int8 and several 4-bit quantization paths; we have preset profiles but sometimes you need a light recompile for the model or a conversion step. We can test with one of your representative models.
[05:48] Miguel Santos: Are there licensing restrictions or special builds for the kernels?
[05:52] Priya Rao: Nothing vendor-locked on our side; optimization kernels are chosen at runtime. Some partners want precompiled kernels that are tuned for their hardware, which we can support by shipping a kernel bundle to your AMI.

[06:20] [00:380] Ethan Morales: Quick note on caching — Redwood's prefix and KV cache can live in-memory on the node or in an external Redis. On partner pools we often prefer to keep small local KV caches to avoid cross-VPC egress. Any constraints?
[06:33] Priya Desai: We allow ephemeral node-local storage, but we also have a managed Redis inside the same VPC. Egress across VPC is allowed but sometimes incurs peering limits.
[06:44] Priya Rao: Okay that works. For low-latency use cases we recommend node-local KV where possible. We can provide a small agent to manage cache warming.

[07:05] [00:450] Jonah Kim: About throughput — if a customer expects 1k QPS for a 2-token average prompt, what does Redwood recommend for instance sizing?
[07:15] Priya Rao: It depends on model size. For an Llama2-13B-ish with quantization and batching, you might see 120-250 qps per A100-class GPU under steady state depending on batching. For that QPS you'd want a pool of maybe 6-8 GPUs with autoscale buffers. We'll prepare a rough right-sizing estimate.
[07:36] Miguel Santos: Autoscales — do you support burst capacity and cross-region fallback?
[07:42] Ethan Morales: Yes. Redwood Dedicated has burst and fallback policies; we can configure regional fallback to another Alder Arc pool or to a Redwood-hosted pool if the partner pool is saturated.

[08:10] [00:520] Priya Desai: Curious about observability — we need logs, traces, and token-level cost breakdown. How does Redwood surface that?
[08:18] Priya Rao: Redwood Console provides per-model and per-route dashboards, token latency, and cost breakdowns. We can also forward traces to your tracing endpoint or S3. For pilots, a minimal dashboard with key KPIs is usually enough.

[08:45] Jonah Kim: Onboarding — what's the minimum baseline to get a bench running?
[08:50] Ethan Morales: Typically: 1) test AMI with drivers, 2) a staging VPC peering, 3) small set of representative models + workload, 4) credentials for a short-lived sandbox. We can stand up the Redwood agent in under a day if the AMI matches our expected runtime environment.

[09:20] [00:600] Miguel Santos: Any gotchas you've seen with partners?
[09:24] Priya Rao: A common issue is mismatched CUDA/cuDNN versions causing slower kernels or crashes. Also network MTU/fragmentation can spike latency for large requests. We document these in our partner runbook.

[09:40] Sofie Laurent: Re SOC2 and compliance, we'll need a gap map — specifically SSO/SAML, audit logs, and data retention.
[09:47] Ethan Morales: We'll share our SOC2 artifact set and a mapping template. For customers that require more we usually do an in-depth control mapping session.

[10:05] [00:650] Jonah Kim: Let's talk pilot timeline. We want to run a 2-week sandbox with a couple of customers. What's realistic?
[10:13] Ethan Morales: Realistic: 1 week to get peering and AMI validated, then 2 weeks benchmark + perf tuning. So plan for a 3-week start-to-results cadence. We can compress but we'd prefer not to.

[10:35] Priya Desai: Regarding AMI, we can build a image with your agent and expose it to a staging account. Is the agent intrusive?
[10:42] Priya Rao: It's a standard container + small init service; it doesn't require root modifications beyond the driver install which you already have. We can also ship a tested AMI if that helps.

[11:00] [00:700] Miguel Santos: A partner commercial question — when customers consume Alder Arc via Redwood, do you embed us in the console?
[11:07] Ethan Morales: The Console can show partner capacity as an option in the deployment route. We can co-brand or list as a private capacity provider. The billing path is up to the GTM agreement.

[11:30] [00:740] Jonah Kim: One technical detail — how do you manage model version pinning and rollouts on partner infrastructure?
[11:38] Priya Rao: Rollouts are handled by our orchestration layer; you can pin model versions per route. For partner nodes we respect pinned artifact URIs and deploy identical bundles. We also support canary and A/B rollouts with automatic fallback to a known-good variant.

[12:05] Priya Desai: Do you need any special network ports open besides gRPC/HTTPS?
[12:10] Priya Rao: Mainly control plane HTTPS (443), gRPC for traffic — we also use a small heartbeat port 15001 for health (can be proxied). We'll provide a whitelist.

[12:35] [00:800] Ethan Morales: Quick audible — Priya, can you run us through the kernel autodetect flow? Just the high-level so Alder Arc understands the probe.
[12:43] Priya Rao: Sure. On startup the runtime queries the CUDA driver and device attributes, runs a fast micro-benchmark for a few kernels, and then selects a kernel bundle. If the probe fails we'll fall back to a general-purpose kernel at lower perf but higher stability. It takes a few seconds.
[13:05] Jonah Kim: Okay that makes sense.

[13:30] [00:840] Miguel Santos: A small nit — in our onboarding we try to avoid any outbound connections to the internet from compute nodes. Is that compatible?
[13:37] Priya Rao: Yes — we support fully private mode where the node only talks to your control plane endpoints over the peered network; we can avoid public egress. That however limits auto-updates unless you provide an update bucket.

[14:05] Sofie Laurent: For audit logs, can we push to your S3 or do you prefer us to ingest?
[14:10] Ethan Morales: We can accept ingestion to your S3 with a signed short-term URL, or we can forward logs to your SIEM. We'll document both options.

[14:30] [00:900] Jonah Kim: Any examples of partners with similar integration?
[14:33] Priya Rao: We've done similar integrations with two regional cloud partners where we ran our agent on partner AMIs and used local KV caches. The main learnings were around driver parity and reducing cross-VPC chatter.

[15:00] Miguel Santos: For the pilot, we'd like Redwood to run a quick compatibility pass with our staging AMI and one of the customer's small models. Is that OK?
[15:07] Ethan Morales: Yes — that's exactly what we propose. Priya can run the bench and we'll share a short perf matrix.

[15:30] [00:960] Priya Rao: To be efficient, please provide a staging account and an AMI ID. We'll consume that and run a simple dockerized workload and report back.
[15:40] Jonah Kim: We'll do that. Also, we'll include the driver versions and the NVLink topology doc.

[16:10] Priya Desai: About model artifacts, can Redwood pull from a private S3 or do you require a container registry?
[16:18] Priya Rao: We support both. We pull artifacts from S3 with IAM roles or from private registries via credentials. For pilot S3 is easiest.

[16:45] [00:1020] Sofie Laurent: On data residency, we have EU customers — do you support region locking for logs and telemetry?
[16:52] Ethan Morales: Yes, data residency is supported in Redwood Dedicated; we can keep logs and telemetry in-region and restrict backups. We'll map that in the POC.

[17:20] Miguel Santos: Any performance tuning we should anticipate?
[17:24] Priya Rao: We'll likely tune batch size, KV cache warmup, and kernel selection. Sometimes a small change in MTU or kernel flags moves latency down by 10-20%.

[17:45] [00:1080] Ethan Morales: Alright, let's capture next steps. I'll send the integration checklist and a sample runbook. Priya (Redwood) will do the AMI compatibility pass, and Alder Arc will provide AMI ID, staging account, and model artifacts.
[17:58] Jonah Kim: Sounds good. We'll aim to have those by 2026-10-21.

[18:15] Priya Rao: We'll also include a brief perf doc and an initial right-size recommendation.
[18:22] Sofie Laurent: I'll compile security questions and send them back to Ethan by 10/24.

[18:40] Ethan Morales: Great. Any final Qs?
[18:45] Miguel Santos: One small point — for billing and marketplace options, we'll chat with your GTM but initial pilot partner-billed is fine.
[18:53] Ethan Morales: Perfect. We'll coordinate GTM internally and loop you in.

[19:10] Jonah Kim: Thank you all, this was really helpful.
[19:15] Ethan Morales: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the checklist and a calendar invite for the scoping call.

Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., K-V cash for KV cache, 'autodetect' transcribed as 'auto deck'), filler words retained. References to attachments: "partner runbook", "AMI spec", "NVLink topology".
